MN202610_131vwxaw0jw.t:
GISAGARA : Amakuru UMUSEKE wamenye avuga ko Umuyobozi w’Akarere wungirije Ushinzwe Imibereho myiza y’abaturage, Dusabe Denise n’Ukuriye RIB, DCI, bafunzwe.

Amakuru UMUSEKE ukesha imboni zawo ziri muri aka Karere avuga ko Inzego z’Ubugenzacyaha zataye muri yombi Visi Meya, Dusabe Denise n’Umuyobozi wa RIB muri aka Karere, Rangira Anicet bafunzwe bakekwaho ko bafatanywe ruswa ya miliyoni 4 y’amafaranga y’u Rwanda.

Abatanze amakuru bavuga ko izo miliyoni 4 Frw bari bazihawe n’Umukomisiyoneri Padiri w’imwe muri Paruwasi yo mu Idini Gatolika yo muri aka Karere yari yohereje.

Ayo makuru akavuga ko aba bayobozi bombi bamenye amakuru ko hari umuterankunga wahaye uyu Padiri miliyoni zirenga 20 zo gusana Ishuri, ayakubita umufuka.

Umwe mu batanze amakuru yagize ati: “Bamaze kumenya ko Padiri atagikoresheje iyo nkunga bamwotsa igitutu bashaka ko bayagabana kugeza ubwo yemeye ko aza kubaha izo miliyoni 4Frw.”

Uwatanze amakuru yabwiye UMUSEKE ko bashyizeho Komisiyoneri, Padiri amaze kuyamuha uyu mugabo ahamagara aba bayobozi ababwira ko abazaniye ayo mafaranga bamubwira aho abasanga, atangiye kuyabaha RIB ibagwa gitumo ihita ibafunga.

Visi Meya Dusabe Denise yari arangije Manda y’imyaka 5, ubu yari ku rutonde rw’abakandida bahatanira kwiyamamariza umwanya w’abajyanama rusange b’Akarere ka Gisagara.

Abatanze amakuru bavuga ko bataramenya niba Padiri wahaye abo Bayobozi ruswa ariwe wongeye gutanga amakuru ko Visi Meya n’Umuyobozi wa RIB barimo kumwaka ruswa cyangwa niba Inzego z’Ubugenzacyaha zari zamenye ko Dusabe na DCI batangiye gusaba uyu Muyobozi wa Paruwasi ruswa y’ayo mafaranga.

MN202610_4ua1xi2vxg.t:
Umuhanzi w’icyamamare muri Tanzania, Diamond Platnumz, yatangaje ko agiye gushyira hanze indirimbo nshya yakoranye n’Umunyarwanda The Ben, nyuma y’imyaka ine bombi basohoye indirimbo ‘Why’yamenyekanye cyane muri Afurika y’Iburasirazuba.

Diamond Platnumz yabitangaje ubwo yari yitabiriye ibirori byo kwizihiza imyaka 10 ya Comedy Store Uganda.

Yavuze ko indirimbo nshya yakoranye na The Ben izasohoka mu gihe cya vuba, bituma abakunzi b’aba bahanzi barushaho kugira amatsiko yo kumenya igihe izagerera hanze.

The Ben na Diamond Platnumz basanzwe bafitanye ubucuti n’imikoranire ishingiye ku kubahana no gushyigikirana. Ibi byagaragaye cyane mu ndirimbo yabo ‘Why’ yasohotse mu 2022, ikishimirwa n’abakunzi b’umuziki mu karere.

Aba bahanzi kandi bahuriye ku rubyiniro mu bitaramo bitandukanye, birimo Trace Awards ya 2023.

The Ben ni umwe mu bahanzi bakomeye mu Rwanda, ufite indirimbo zikundwa cyane ndetse n’imikoranire n’abahanzi bo mu karere ka Afurika y’Iburasirazuba no hanze yako.

Muri Kanama 2026, Diamond Platnumz yongeye kugaragaza ko afata The Ben nk’umuvandimwe we.

Yanavuze ko yifuzaga ko bahurira ku rubyiniro i Kigali, ariko ntibyakunda kubera izindi gahunda The Ben yari afite muri Uganda.

Indirimbo nshya y’aba bahanzi itegerejwe na benshi, byitezwe ko izongera guhuza abakunzi b’umuziki mu Rwanda, Tanzania, Uganda no mu bindi bihugu byo muri Afurika y’Iburasirazuba.

MN202610_11c065gkg8y.t:
Nyuma y’igihe hari amakimbirane hagati ya Yago Pon Dat na Bruce Melodie yatumye Shene ya Yago Tv Show ikurwa ku muyoboro wa Youtube, kuri ubu yagarutse bigizwemo uruhare n’ubuhuza bwakozwe n’umunyamakuru Jado Castar.

Mu 2025, nibwo umubano w’aba bombi watangiye kuzamo agatotsi, ubwo Yago yanengaga Bruce Melodie ku mbuga nkoranyambaga.

Mu 2026, amakimbirane yafashe indi ntera hagati yabo nyuma y’uko Yago anenze indirimbo ‘Irya 4’ ya Bruce Melodie, na we akamusubiza agaragaza ko atishimiye amagambo yamuvuzeho.

Ku wa 13 Ukwakira 2026, Yago Pon Dat yatangaje ko shene ye ya YouTube, Yago TV Show, yari imaze guhabwa ibihano bitatu kubera ibirego by’ihohoterwa ry’uburenganzira ku mutungo bwite mu by’ubwenge, bijyanye n’amashusho y’ibiganiro yari yaragiranye na Bruce Melodie. Yashinjaga uyu muhanzi n’ikipe ye kuba ari bo bari inyuma y’ibyo birego.

Yagize ati: “Bruce Melodie n’ikipe bamaze kurega Yago TV Show nanone, aho noneho bifashishije ibiganiro bitandukanye twakoranye na we mu bihe bitandukanye. Ubu tuvugana, Yago TV Show bayihaye Strike eshatu, hasigaye iminsi umunani ngo isibwe ku rubuga rwa YouTube.”

Bruce Melodie yasobanuye ko ibirego byatumye Yago TV Show ihabwa ibihano byatanzwe n’ikipe ye ndetse n’ikigo cyaguze uburenganzira bwo gucuruza album ye ‘Colorful Generation’, bitewe n’uko indirimbo ziri kuri iyo album zakoreshwaga mu mashusho Yago yashyiraga kuri shene ye.

Yavuze ko atifuzaga ko Yago ahomba amaramuko, amusaba kwegera abatanze ibirego bakaganira kugira ngo ikibazo gikemuke. Yanamusezeranyije kumufasha kugikemura.

Ku wa 16 Ukwakira 2026, Jado Castar yatangaje ko amaze kuganira na Yago amasaha agera kuri abiri. Nyuma y’icyo kiganiro, Yago yemeye amakosa yakoze, asaba imbabazi ku magambo n’ibikorwa byatewe n’umujinya.

Izo mbabazi yanazisabge Abanyarwanda n’abandi bose baba barababajwe n’imvugo ze.

Nyuma yaho, Jado Castar yatangaje ko Bruce Melodie yahaye imbabazi Yago Pon Dat, agaragaza ko kubabarira umuntu wakugiriye nabi ari ikimenyetso cy’ubutwari n’ubumuntu.

Yagize ati: “Gutanga imbabazi si ugutsindwa, ni ubumuntu bw’igisagirane. Uba ubaye intangarugero, ni wowe uba ufite icyo utanga, urakagihorana.”

Ku wa 22 Ukwakira 2026, shene ya Yago TV Show nibwo yari yahagaritswe burundu kuri YouTube, ariko iza kongera gukora ku wa 29 Ukwakira 2026, nyuma y’iminsi irindwi idakora.

Kuri uyu wa 30 Ukwakira 2026, Yago yanditse ku mbuga nkoranyambaga ubutumwa bugira buti: “Muvandimwe wanjye Bruce Melodie ndagusuhuje. Ubu ni ubutumwa ntanze ku mugaragaro, mbuvanye ku mutima kandi nicishije bugufi. Nongeye kugusaba imbabazi by’ukuri ku byabaye hagati yacu. ririya hangana ntiryari bikenewe. Uracyari umuvandimwe wanjye, nanjye ndi umuvandimwe wawe, uko ibintu byaba bimeze kose.Urakoze mwami Bruce Melodie (B.M).”

Ubushinjacyaha bwasabiye abakozi ba RMB gufungwa by’agateganyo kubera ibyaha bubakurikiranyeho.

Ubushinjacyaha bwasabiye Uwamamhoro Fiona na Assoumani Bienfait abakozi ba RMB gufungwa iminsi 30 by’agateganyo kubera ibyaha byo kutamenyekanisha icyaha cy’ubugome cyangwa gikomeye, icyo kuba icyitso mu cyaha cyo kwiba, no kuba icyitso cyo gukora Ubucukuzi bw’amabuye y’agaciro nta ruhushya.

Iburanisha ryasubukuwe ku mugoroba wo kuri uyu Kane taliki ya 29/10/2026 nyuma yuko Abunganira Uwamamhoro Fiona na mugenzi we Assoumani Bienfait bagaragarije Urukiko rw’Ibanze rwa Nyamabuye ko imyanzuro y’ibyaha Ubushinjacyaha burega abakiliya babo batigeze bayibona muri sisitemu y’ikoranabuhanga rikoreshwa mu nkiko.

Ubushinjacyaha buvuga ko Uwamamhoro Fiona na Assoumani bagiye gukora ubugenzuzi muri Kampani yitwa Rugendabari Mining kandi yarahagaritswe.

Ubushinjacyaha bukavuga ko usibye guhagarikwa, aba bakozi ba RMB bahageze basanga hari ibyapa n’impuzankano by’abayirinda byanditseho Rugendabari Mining Company Ltd bakomeza akazi ko kugenzura batabyitayeho.

Ubushinjacyaha buvuga ko usibye ibi, aba bakozi bagiye gukora ubugenzuzi taliki ya 11/06/2026 hashyira amezi abiri bataratanga raporo.

Umushinjacyaha yagize ati: “Ubusabe bw’Ubushinjacyaha ni uko bafungwa iminsi 30 y’agateganyo kubera ko iperereza rikomeje.”

Abaregwa bahakanye ibyaha bashinjwa bakavuga ko igenzura bakoze ryakorewe Kampani yitwa SEAVMC ko batigeze bajya muri Rugendabari Mining Company Ltd kuko n’ubutumwa bw’akazi bwavugaga ko bagomba gukora ubugenzuzi muri SEAVMC.

Abaregwa n’ababunganira babwiye Urukiko ko ibijyanye n’ibyapa babihasanze kandi ibyo bashinjwa batabyemera.

Bavuga ko guhagarika Kampani biri mu bubasha bwabo.

Ubushinjacyaha bwongeraho ko hari n’igitabo cy’abashyitsi cya Kampani ya Rugendabari basinyemo ndetse batanga n’inama (Recommandation).

Abaregwa bavuga ko habayeho ikosa mu gusinya muri iki gitabo, ariko ko bitagombye kuba bigize ibyaha bingana gutya bashinjwa.

Bagasaba ko barekurwa by’agateganyo bagakurikiranwa bari hanze ndetse bagategekwa ibyo bagomba kubahiriza bitabangamira iperereza.

Gusa nubwo bimeze bityo Ubushinjacyaha mu iburanisha ribanza, buvuga ko bwabajije Ubuyobozi bwa RMB ko SEAVMC ifite uruhushya mu Karere ka Muhanga, burahakana.

Ubushinjacyaha kandi bwabajije aba bakozi kubereka ikimenyetso kigaragaza ko ari SEAVMC basuye ariko ntibakigaragaza.

Isomwa ry’urubanza kuri iki cyemezo kizasomwa taliki ya 03/11/2026 saa kumi z’umugoroba.

MN202610_1jvee1w7aiq.t:
The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is often rated as one of the greatest video games

The moment she saw footage from the remake of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time, Kacey Doran picked up her phone. She had to tell her sister.

"Have you seen this?" messaged Doran, excitedly.

Nearly 30 years ago, a 10-year-old Doran had sat in front of her family's TV, reading out the dialogue on screen to her sister, a year younger, as they inched their way through the original Nintendo 64 game's sprawling, puzzle-filled dungeons. Ocarina's fantasy-like story, and beautiful music, enthralled them both.

It was also the first game Doran ever completed. Now, countless memories rushed back to her as she devoured clips of the fully redesigned version, due to arrive on the Switch 2 later this year.

Doran's sister messaged back: "I'm not tearing up… YOU'RE tearing up."

News of a video game remake bought back happy memories for Kacey Doran

This is the power of nostalgia – and a perfect example of how video games can trigger it. Doran now teaches an esports course at Rowan University in New Jersey. She says the original Ocarina of Time, released in 1998, had a "magical" quality that she hopes to rediscover, and also share with her sister's children.

The video games industry has long leaned on remakes. From Mario Kart to the Final Fantasy series, or even Pac-Man, some games just keep coming back in updated forms, as new generations of gamers emerge and as computer hardware improves, enabling more detailed graphics and increasingly expansive game worlds.

While the emotional hook may be the most significant draw, putting out a remake can be a double-edged sword. Some gamers are very protective of their favourite titles and new versions don't always meet certain fans' astronomically high expectations.

Nostalgia is an important but mixed emotion, says Tim Wulf, at the Centre for Advanced Internet Studies in Bochum, Germany. It has positive aspects but also a kind of sadness, too. Happiness in remembering things that were important to us, and also an awareness that that time is now gone.

"It's a social emotion because memories that induce nostalgia for us are connected to other people," he explains, adding that nostalgia can boost our self-esteem while highlighting key social bonds.

Video games, says Wulf, are notoriously good at triggering nostalgia because gamers can "jump into the same environment". In other words, games are like time machines for our emotions, and returning to fondly remembered places can feel stabilising or reassuring in an ever-changing world.

Doran, for one, notes that when you return to a favourite old game, there's something satisfying about deploying previously learned skills. You know what to do here, you're winning again. Just like the old days.

Video games are good at triggering nostalgic feelings says Tim Wulf

Putting out remasters and remakes has been a "really successful" strategy for the games industry, says Piers Harding-Rolls, head of games research at Ampere Analysis.

"Tying in with established audiences and building on existing content is quite a safe route for a lot of companies," he adds. In many cases, it is cheaper to update an existing game rather than create a new title from scratch.

Among other remakes that have found big audiences recently are those of Resident Evil 4 and Assassin's Creed Black Flag.

But Ocarina of Time perhaps stands out because, ever since its original release, it has been considered by many as one of the greatest games ever made. "The interest from all the Gen Zs that I work with is really high," says Harding-Rolls. The legend of The Legend of Zelda, as it were.

Since 2007 there have been 14 main releases of Assassin's Creed

Clearly, nostalgia is not the only driver of interest in the remake, and today's audiences will expect a game that plays to today's standards.

Games companies must keep innovating when linking contemporary audiences to the past, says Wulf, in order satisfy their desire for fresh experiences. And although Wulf himself was a big fan of the original, he has no personal interest in the Ocarina of Time remake. "I want a new game – I don't want to play an old game," he says. Nostalgia isn't always enough for some.

Plus, critics often highlight a tension between originals and remakes. Which is the definitive version? In 2021, Square Enix released the bizarrely titled Nier Replicant ver.1.22474487139... – a remaster of a game first published in 2010. One reviewer wrote , external , "What we're left with is two nearly identical Niers each vying to be the true Nier."

Fans may react badly should a remaster or remake fail to do justice to the source material. And, in the gaming world, angry fan reactions can be serious .

"There's always going to be that fan base or group of people that are going to nit-pick," says Stephanie Ijoma, chief executive and founder of NNESAGA, a consultancy and creative agency.

Ultimately, games developers working on remakes have to "find the right balance" between appealing to fans and allowing themselves to be creative with the material, she adds. "You can't make art in fear, you can't create in fear."

Ijoma gives the example of Final Fantasy VII. First released in 1997, it got a highly anticipated remake in 2020.

This was a game Ijoma played back in the late 1990s and she was thrilled to be able to share it with younger players today.

First released in 1997, Final Fantasy VII got a remake in 2020

Remakes enable this sharing of experiences because getting old computer hardware or video games consoles to work, while a pastime loved by some , is not possible for everyone.

"I've tried multiple times to play Silent Hill 2 because I'm interested in older games but it's such a difficult game to come into nowadays," says Niklas Hallin, a solo indie game developer who runs the studio Neckbolt. "They made a remake and it's so smooth, it just works. It works on your modern hardware."

Hallin did not play many games as a child so he says nostalgia isn't much of a motivator for him. However, in his own games, he likes to include subtle stylistic references to classic games because he knows that this appeals to gamers.

Indie developers often lean on retro games aesthetics not just because people respond well to them – but also because they are easier to achieve. "You can't compete with billion dollar budgets, super high-fidelity, Triple A graphics," he says.

One question remains. The visual difference, today, between games released years apart is, arguably, negligible. So will there be any point in remaking a game from 2026 in, say, 2038? Will technology have moved on so much by then that it's actually worth it?

Harding-Rolls predicts that games companies will still seek to connect new audiences with classic titles by offering updates.

Remakes might become less about graphical improvements and more about editorial adjustments. "Reinterpretations," he says. "Or versions with additional content."

Sir Patrick Stewart, who has died at the age of 86, was a stage and screen great who balanced Hollywood stardom with an equally stellar career in classical theatre.

While many actors are typecast, he moved effortlessly from Shakespeare and Dickens to the command of the USS Enterprise and his famous wheelchair in X-Men.

In a career that spanned seven decades, Sir Patrick received multiple awards, a star on the Hollywood Walk of Fame and a knighthood from Queen Elizabeth II.

One of the world's most versatile actors, he mastered both comedy and tragedy, science-fiction and historical drama - despite the entertainment industry's traditional dislike of bald heads.

Sir Ian McKellen leads tributes to 'beloved actor' Sir Patrick Stewart after his death at 86

From watching Star Trek to knighthood - Sir Patrick Stewart's memorable BBC moments

Patrick Hewes Stewart was born in Mirfield in the West Riding of Yorkshire on 13 July 1940.

His mother Gladys was a textile worker. She was active in amateur dramatics and encouraged her three sons to take part.

His father was a former Sergeant Major in the Parachute Regiment whose experience during the wartime evacuation of Dunkirk had shredded his mental health.

"My father was a very potent individual," Stewart later recalled. "It was said that when he strode on to the parade ground, birds stopped singing."

But Alfred Stewart had become a quick-tempered man, suffering from what would now be called post traumatic stress.

He was prone to drink and often took out his frustrations on his family - although Patrick himself was never the target of his fists.

Star Trek actor Sir Patrick Stewart dies aged 86

Follow updates: Tributes paid to Sir Patrick Stewart

'A big loss' - Fans react to death of Sir Patrick Stewart

Patrick Stewart in the Royal Shakespeare Company's 1970 production of The Two Gentlemen of Verona

Young Patrick's love of drama developed at school when one of his teachers introduced him to Shakespeare and encouraged him to perform.

His first public performance was in a local church production of Cinderella.

He found the predictability of dramatic performances a welcome change from the turmoil of his home life.

He left school at 15 and eventually got a job as a journalist and obituary writer on the Dewsbury Reporter.

He also threw himself enthusiastically into the flourishing local theatre. "I used to recite Shakespeare from memory," he said. "I just learned all these big speeches."

He played a conspiratorial Roman soldier in the BBC's I, Claudius in 1976

But he found it impossible to concentrate on both his job and his acting. Eventually his editor told him to choose between journalism and the "foolhardy" acting.

Stewart picked up his typewriter and walked out.

At the age of 18, he had the traumatic experience of losing all his hair, a huge blow to an aspiring actor and self-conscious teenager - who worried that girls would no longer find him attractive.

He won a scholarship to the Bristol Old Vic and later joined the Royal Shakespeare Company - playing a variety of roles across the company's repertoire.

And when not appearing as Oberon or Enobarbus, he made his TV debut as a fireman in a 1967 episode of soap opera Coronation Street.

Patrick Stewart as a Russian spy in 1982 BBC series Smiley's People

His Broadway debut came in 1970 as Snout in Peter Brook's critically acclaimed production of A Midsummer Night's Dream.

Over the next two decades, Stewart appeared in a variety of television roles without threatening to become a major star.

In 1974, he played Lenin in the BBC's 13-part drama series The Fall of Eagles.

He was a conspiratorial Roman soldier in the hugely popular I, Claudius and a Soviet spy in Tinker, Tailor, Soldier, Spy and Smiley's People.

Watch: "A big loss" - Fans react to death of Sir Patrick Stewart

In 1984, Stewart left the RSC and moved to the National Theatre. By then in his mid-40s, he had only ever been unemployed for three weeks, but was rarely cast as a main character.

He had landed a number of supporting film roles: including playing Guinevere's father in Excalibur, a warrior-minstrel in Dune, and a riding instructor in Little Lord Fauntleroy.

And he was the voice of a small character in the animated film of Richard Adams' novel The Plague Dogs.

But even he described the first half of his career as "sound but never spectacular".

His career really took off aboard the USS Enterprise as Captain Jean-Luc Picard in Star Trek: The Next Generation

Then came the role of Captain Jean-Luc Picard.

A producer named Robert L Justman was intent on reviving the Star Trek franchise, and was looking for a successor to William Shatner's legendary James T Kirk.

He had hoped to find a sexy, hirsute Frenchman to play the role - but chanced upon Stewart giving a lecture to his wife's Shakespeare class in Los Angeles.

Justman turned to his wife. "I said I think I've found our new captain," he said.

He knew nothing about the original Star Trek and his great friend, Sir Ian McKellen, told him not to throw his stage career away on a wild goose chase into space.

But in need of a boost to his finances, Stewart signed a six-year contract, firmly believing the show wouldn't last and he'd be back on the boards before long.

Patrick Stewart and the cast of Star Trek: The Next Generation

"Everybody told me it would be a flop," he recalled. "A friend of mine said, 'Get a suntan, make some money, go home.'"

He was, however, pleased that the producers didn't mind his baldness.

He'd tried wearing a wig in early screen tests, but it looked ratty and - in the end - Star Trek's founder Gene Roddenberry told him to ditch it.

"In the 24th Century, they wouldn't care if Picard was bald," he said.

Stewart, who was billed by the New York Times as "an unknown British Shakespearean actor", found it hard adapting to his new job.

After his stage experiences, he found the 20 hours a day on set tiring, and he also struggled to work with a fairly laid-back and fun-loving US cast.

His decision to call his fellow actors together and give them a lecture about behaving more seriously failed to gain him popularity.

Sir Ian McKellen and Sir Patrick Stewart were the best of friends as well as co-stars

"It was really awful, being dressed down by the captain," said Brent Spiner, who played Data, the android. "We really thought, 'Well, please, get over it'."

Eventually Stewart softened, insisting that every member of the cast told at least one joke a day.

Despite his initial reservations, Star Trek: The Next Generation both survived and prospered - making its star a very wealthy man.

Captain Picard was supposed to be French, but displayed a surprisingly English regard for both Shakespeare and Earl Grey tea.

And, after playing all those Shakespearean princes and dukes on the London stage, Stewart became fiercely proud of him, and of the show's ability to connect with younger audiences.

Sir Patrick starred as the telepathic Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men film franchise

In addition to the television series, Stewart played Picard in four Star Trek films. But while commanding the Enterprise, he managed to not neglect the theatre.

With his new-found celebrity, the parts he was offered improved greatly.

For years, he performed a one-man version of Charles Dickens' A Christmas Carol on Broadway - playing all 40 characters.

In 1995, he appeared as Prospero in a memorable performance of The Tempest and, two years later, he starred as Othello - who he presented as a white mercenary in a black African nation.

But his Star Trek success limited the roles that Hollywood was prepared to offer him.

"No director wanted to cast this grand, deep-voiced, bald English guy," he told the Times. "Because everybody knew he was Picard and couldn't possibly be anybody else."

Sir Ian and Sir Patrick appeared together in Waiting for Godot

Eventually, he took the role of Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men film franchise, essentially playing a telepathic Picard in a wheelchair.

His co-star was Sir Ian McKellen - the friend who'd warned him to avoid Hollywood - in the metal-bending role of Magneto.

Alongside his work in America, he won critical acclaim opposite Harriet Walter in Antony and Cleopatra in 2007.

And, in the same year, he played Macbeth for the first time - despite a 30-year age gap between him and Kate Fleetwood, playing Lady Macbeth.

Critic Nicholas de Jongh decided it was "the best Macbeth I have ever seen", and hailed him as "one of our finest Shakespearean actors".

In 2010, Stewart was awarded a knighthood for his services to drama.

Sir Patrick Stewart received his knighthood in 2010

In 2009, he again teamed up with Sir Ian in Waiting For Godot.

It was a moment of personal fulfilment for Sir Patrick who, as an awed teenager, remembered watching Peter O'Toole in the play at the Bristol Old Vic.

His deep and authoritative voice made him much in demand for voice-over roles - including a reprise of his role as Captain Jean-Luc Picard on Star Trek video games.

One female interviewer once gushed that "just hearing him order breakfast is rather thrilling".

He also voiced a host of TV commercials both in Britain and the US.

Away from acting, he was a passionate political activist and a long-time supporter of the Labour Party, as well as a campaigner for victims of domestic abuse.

Sir Patrick Stewart and his wife Sunny Ozell photographed in 2024

In 2013, he married his third wife - singer-songwriter Sunny Ozell - in Nevada.

Sir Ian McKellen officiated at the ceremony, which had to be restaged at a Los Angeles restaurant when someone discovered that his legal power to do so did not extend to the Silver State.

A year later, the two knights took their talents to Broadway, alternating performances of Waiting for Godot with Harold Pinter's No Man's Land.

Sir Patrick made a video for Amnesty International on the subject of domestic violence, referencing his father's brutality towards his mother.

Once named the third greatest Yorkshireman after Michael Palin and Sean Bean, he never lost touch with his roots - keeping a house in God's Own Country, and remaining a lifelong supporter of Huddersfield Town football club.

Forthcoming projects had included a final performance as Professor Charles Xavier in Marvel's Avengers: Doomsday, which will be released this Christmas.

And, if millions remember him only as the somewhat taciturn commander of the USS Enterprise, that prospect was not something that worried him.

"For huge numbers of people I will always be Jean-Luc Picard, and that's fine," he said. "I really believe we created an admirable individual."

From watching Star Trek to knighthood - Sir Patrick Stewart's memorable BBC moments

Legendary actor Sir Patrick Stewart rose from humble beginnings in his native Yorkshire to become a global superstar whose work became immortalised portraying characters on some of the most popular sci-fi franchises in history.

The star, who won acclaim on both stages and screens, died at his home in Los Angeles on Thursday after a career that spanned more than seven decades. He was 86.

Sir Ian McKellen leads tributes to 'beloved actor' Sir Patrick Stewart after his death at 86

Sir Patrick Stewart: Actor who moved effortlessly between Star Trek and Shakespeare

'A big loss' - Fans react to death of Sir Patrick Stewart

Born in 1940, his mother was a textile worker and his father was a former military officer whose experience during the wartime evacuation of Dunkirk had a profound impact on his mental health.

Baby Patrick seen being held by his Aunt Dolly. He is seen with his mother (right) and brothers Trevor (left) and Geoff

He grew up poor, and later spoke to journalists about witnessing his mother being abused by his father.

Stewart (right) pictured with his brother Trevor and his mother, circa 1945

Young Patrick's love of drama came at school when one of his teachers introduced him to Shakespeare and encouraged him to perform.

Stewart played Launce for Robin Phillips' production of 'Two Gentlemen Of Verona' in London in 1970

He threw himself enthusiastically into the flourishing local theatre. "I used to recite Shakespeare from memory," he said. "I just learned all these big speeches."

He went on to star in countless Shakespeare plays. One of his earliest breakout roles was in 1970's Two Gentlemen of Verona, which also featured his rescue dog, Blackie, playing the role of the dog Crab.

Stewart played Sejanus in the 1976 BBC historical drama series I, Claudius

His expertise in Shakespeare led to play a major role in the 1976 BBC television series I, Claudius.

In 1981, he was featured in 1981 fantasy film Excalibur, bringing him one step closer to his future sci-fi career.

Stewart (far right) played Leondegrance in the film Excalibur

Sir Patrick has won numerous awards, including a Grammy and two Laurence Olivier Awards. He was also nominated for a Tony, along with multiple Golden Globes and Emmys over the years.

His iconic voice and facial expressions saw him star in both the Star Trek and X-Men franchises, helping to spawn a generation of global sci-fi fans.

Stewart played Jean-Luc Picard, the commanding officer of the Federation starship USS Enterprise, on Star Trek

In 1987, he took on the role of Jean-Luc Picard on popular TV series Star Trek: The Next Generation. Tapping into Star Trek fandom earned him millions of adoring fans around the world.

Star Trek: The Next Generation started airing in 1987 and spanned 178 episodes over seven seasons.

Sir Patrick starred in a 2008 Broadway performance of Shakespeare's Macbeth

Queen Elizabeth II knighted Sir Patrick at Buckingham Palace in 2010

Sir Patrick poses with his knighthood medal

His scores of sci-fi fans reached new heights with his starring role as Professor Charles Xavier in the X-Men film series, which began in 2000.

He reprised the role multiple times over decades through the Marvel Cinematic Universe, including in 2026 in Avengers: Doomsday.

Stewart gained scores of new fans with his portrayal of Professor X in X-Men

Stewart appeared alongside X-Men co-stars Hugh Jackman (left) and Ian McKellen (right)

Eating fruit and vegetable scraps such as peels and stalks could provide a health boost that most of us are missing, say UK researchers , external .

They say scraps are an overlooked source of dietary fibre and are encouraging people to try "root-to-tip" eating, including watermelon rind, pineapple core and butternut squash seeds.

Most adults do not get enough fibre. Official figures , external show only 4% meet the recommended 30g a day, despite its well-known benefits for gut health.

Fibre aids digestion, helps you feel fuller for longer and is linked to a lower risk of heart disease and bowel cancer. , external

Skin and pips can be beneficial, the fibre researchers say

As a rule of thumb, the skins of fruit and veg pack more fibre than the insides.

Eating a kiwi with the skin on , external provides 50% more fibre than having a peeled one, for example.

For their study, the scientists at King's College London analysed 12 raw or uncooked fresh foods - beetroot, bell pepper, broccoli, butternut squash, cauliflower, celeriac, curly kale, fennel, kiwi fruit, leek, pineapple and watermelon.

They found many discarded parts contained more fibre than the sections people typically eat.

watermelon rind contained 2.10g of fibre per 100g – roughly equivalent to the fibre in a slice of wholemeal bread

butternut squash skin and seeds contained 9.25g per 100g – nearly as much fibre as a bowl of bran flakes

pineapple skin and core contained five times more fibre than the flesh

broccoli stalks contained fibre, although a bit less than the florets

Fibre is essential for your gut to work properly and helps prevent constipation.

Project lead Dr Rachel Gibson said the findings suggested people are throwing away a significant amount of fibre.

"This isn't just a nutritional loss, it's also a financial one - you're effectively throwing away a substantial portion of what you've paid for."

King's College London has been experimenting in its canteen , external , offering staff and students root-to-tip meals, such as banana skin curry.

At home, people might want to try leaving skins on kiwi fruit, using broccoli stalks in stir-fries or adding bell pepper seeds to dishes, the researchers suggest.

While cooking can change the fibre content, it doesn't usually destroy it all.

Steaming, microwaving or quick sautéing tends to preserve nutrients best .

Gibson said: "This isn't about perfection and this isn't about forcing people to eat unpalatable food – it's about recognising the nutritional value in components we've been conditioned to discard."

She acknowledges some may be hesitant to try it.

Some diners raised concerns during the canteen trial.

Over the nine-week period, "root-to-tip" dishes made up a third of total daily hot menu sales at the university.

Those choosing the new dishes were less likely to finish their meals than diners eating from the conventional menu.

Kirsten Jackson, a dietitian with the British Dietetic Association who specialises in irritable bowel syndrome (IBS), says the food hacks are useful as long as produce is washed thoroughly.

She suggests blending pineapple cores into smoothies, but says the tough skins are not something she would recommend.

Some stalks may need to be cooked or finely chopped to make them more palatable, she adds.

"Just because a broccoli stalk doesn't fit into tonight's meal doesn't mean it needs to go in the bin. Chop it up, freeze it and add it to a soup or stir-fry another day," she said.

She advises increasing fibre intake gradually to avoid bloating, noting that people who have IBS may find it harder to tolerate.

And there are some things to avoid entirely, said the British Nutrition Foundation.

Green potatoes and rhubarb leaves contain toxic compounds, while tough stalks and seeds may not be suitable for young children.

MN202610_1xnvwpgot6a.t:
Watch: "My low Vitamin D levels hit me like a truck"

Twenty-three-year-old Saskia Reeves-Priestley was at work when she suddenly collapsed.

"I just felt really dizzy, really nauseous, was having heart palpitations and was really hot," she says.

Saskia, a special educational needs teacher, was a keen goalkeeper who played football four times a week and felt fit and healthy. While her symptoms are not directly linked to vitamin D deficiency - she realised something was wrong.

Blood tests later showed her level was so low - it was "next to nothing".

In the UK, low vitamin D rates are increasing in some age groups , external - particularly in girls and young women.

According to data from the National Diet and Nutrition Survey, last year nearly a quarter of 11- to 18-year-olds were classed as deficient.

Vitamin D can come from our diet, in foods such as oily fish and meat, or supplements.

But most is made by our body when UV light in sunlight hits the skin. Lower levels of sunlight - depending on where in the world you live or the time of year - decrease the body's ability to produce it.

Covering parts of the body and wearing sunscreen also has an impact - despite their protective advantages.

Those with darker skin need exposure to stronger light to produce the same amount of vitamin D as lighter skin.

Doctors don't routinely offer blood tests to check for vitamin D deficiency, but will offer a supplement if a patient is concerned they might be high risk.

Vitamin D deficiency is linked to the bone disease rickets in babies and infants. In adults it causes a similar weakening of the bone called osteomalacia , external .

"They call it the silent disease," says Dr Suma Uday, a paediatric endocrinologist who wants to raise awareness of the problem.

She warns that vitamin D deficiency in young people and adults is difficult to spot and can be missed or misdiagnosed. Symptoms include fatigue and joint and bone pain.

Uday says: "It's basically silently eating away at the bones, leaving them softened and prone to breaks."

Amaka Osu says she doesn't think many of her friends realise what the symptoms are

Amaka was in the middle of making dinner at her university house in Liverpool when she started shaking.

"I couldn't really see in front of me," she says. Her housemate took her to A&E - later she too would be diagnosed as vitamin D deficient.

Other than feeling tired, she says she had no symptoms: "I'm a 21-year-old student. I've got work and uni - I'm always feeling tired."

She remembers her mother suffering from low vitamin D but says she did not realise it could happen to her.

After taking supplements, Amaka feels a lot better, but she is anxious in case it happens again. "It was scary and I don't want to experience that again."

Uday joins other clinicians and academics who have formed a group - ACT NOW Vitamin D - calling for the threshold at which you are classified as deficient to be raised.

She says that would "catch" more people with low vitamin D and give a more accurate picture of how widespread the issue is. It would also mean they can treat the deficiency earlier, she says.

Uday warns of "a lifelong deficit" in women - in adolescence, then pregnancy, and then the newborn is affected.

"If you don't correct it from the very beginning," she says, "this is going to affect multiple generations."

Saskia Reeves-Priestley plays football four times a week - and had no previous symptoms

"It's shocking," says Prof Martin Hewison, from the University of Birmingham.

He tells me that despite being 100 years on from the discovery of vitamin D "rickets hasn't gone away".

"If we have rickets in the community, there are going to be many more people who are vitamin D deficient."

He says the government should look into wider fortification of food in which vitamins are added to foods during production. Countries like Canada and Sweden have mandatory policies.

In the UK, some foods such as breakfast cereals and spreads are already fortified with vitamin D, but it is voluntary.

During the winter months, people start to lose their vitamin D levels.

"We might have to accept that for certain groups vitamin D supplementation is a matter of course," says Hewison.

Saskia is now taking vitamin D supplements regularly - and is back in goal.

MN202610_1vjokwdhhd7.t:
US Assistant Attorney General Colin M McDonald vowed to pursue all those involved

In May 2024, Francis Mogambi arrived in the United States after winning the Diversity Visa lottery, a programme that gives people from around the world a chance to become permanent residents.

Just over two years later, the Kenyan national found himself at the centre of a US investigation into an alleged nationwide scheme to defraud the federal student aid system.

On 19 October 2026, a grand jury in Nebraska indicted Mogambi on five counts of theft of government money and five counts of aggravated identity theft.

Prosecutors allege that, between November 2025 and May 2026, he worked with associates in Kenya to steal the identities of US citizens and use them to fraudulently enroll fictitious students in American colleges.

Once the fake students were enrolled, Mogambi allegedly diverted their financial aid payments to himself, keeping 30% and sending the remainder to his associates in Kenya.

The intended loss in his case was $20,000 (£15,000), according to prosecutors.

Court documents say Mogambi received $2,000 a week and attempted to recruit another person into the scheme. He allegedly told the individual he needed a business that would allow him to cash larger cheques without paying taxes.

Mogambi was arrested shortly after the indictment was returned and is being held in custody pending trial. He has not yet commented on the allegations against him.

His case forms part of a wider US investigation, dubbed Operation Ghostbusters, into the alleged use of stolen identities to enrol fictitious students at colleges and claim federal financial aid that resulted in a loss of $130m in taxpayers funds.

US authorities say the investigation has so far resulted in five indictments that involved Kenyan nationals, while a further 40 investigations remain open. Hundreds of people have been affected after fraudsters allegedly stole their personally identifiable information (PII) and used it to access federal student aid.

The stolen personal information was sometimes sold online for between $4 and $8, with fraudsters targeting low-income Americans who had never had the opportunity to attend college.

At a news conference on 29 October announcing the first charges in the investigation, Assistant Attorney General Colin M McDonald, who heads the Justice Department's National Fraud Enforcement Division, vowed to pursue those involved.

"If you steal taxpayers' dollars, if you exploit a programme meant to help students, we are resolved to find you and prosecute you," he said.

The Justice Department says those behind the fraud use what is described as "super intelligence" to place fake students in classrooms and complete coursework, creating the impression that they are attending college and allowing financial aid payments to continue.

"The goal is to keep the ghost student in school as long as possible. Semester after semester after semester stealing money from the taxpayers," McDonald said.

But the consequences extend beyond the financial losses suffered by the US government.

People whose identities are stolen can find themselves facing unexpected student loan debts, even if they have never enrolled in college.

"His identity was stolen, his credit is now at risk, and his name is on the bill," McDonald said, describing the impact on one victim.

He also said that nearly a third of community college applicants in California in 2024 had been identified as fraudulent.

The scale of the suspected fraud is significant.

Investigators identified 830,840 potentially fraudulent Federal Student Aid identification numbers associated with nearly $130m in September and October 2026. They recommended that the Department of Education disable them.

The figure represents financial aid associated with potentially fraudulent accounts, not confirmed losses.

"In a flash, the money vanishes, often overseas in places like Kenya," McDonald said.

The investigation has also exposed alleged financial links between the US and Kenya.

In September, US officials travelled to Kenya to work with local law enforcement on extraditions, prosecutions and the recovery of money allegedly stolen from American taxpayers.

With the help of Kenyan investigators, US authorities seized more than $750,000 from a cryptocurrency account belonging to a Kenyan national connected to the wider scheme. The Justice Department described it as the first international seizure of its kind in Kenya.

The seizure was not connected to Mogambi's individual case.

In a separate case in Virginia, prosecutors allege that a Kenyan national received more than 700 fraudulent student-aid refunds totalling approximately $1.44m. At least $1.3m was subsequently transferred through thousands of transactions to accounts in the US and Kenya.

Meanwhile, in New Jersey, three people have been charged with allegedly acting as money mules in a scheme to obtain more than $1m in federal student aid.

Prosecutors say they received the funds through US bank accounts, kept a portion for themselves and transferred the remainder to alleged co-conspirators in Kenya linked to a purported safari company.

If convicted, Mogambi faces a mandatory prison term of at least 10 years, according to the Justice Department.

Authorities say those convicted will also face appropriate orders for forfeiture of assets and restitution to victims, in addition to any prison sentences.

MN202610_12vj48wb1ni.t:
Sadio Mane's Senegal won Afcon 2025 but the result was later overturned in favour of Morocco, and the Court of Arbitration for Sport will determine the ultimate destination of the title

After a shock announcement 10 months ago that the Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) would be held every four years, the governing body of football on the continent has reversed course.

The Confederation of African Football (Caf) will instead retain the tournament's traditional biennial staging, with its president Patrice Motsepe saying the U-turn was based on "advancing, protecting and promoting" the interests of the African game.

The first indication that the frequency of Afcon was being reconsidered came at Caf's strategy conference in Cape Verde earlier this month.

Questions are now being asked about the decision-making process and what this means for the future of African football.

Afcon has predominantly been held every two years since its first edition in 1957, barring two three-year gaps in the 1960s and one year between the 2012 and 2013 tournaments.

On the eve of the 2025 finals in Morocco, Motsepe announced all that would change from 2028.

The South African said the shift to a four-year cycle was, in part, to help the global calendar "be significantly more synchronised and harmonised".

In recent years Afcon has been staged midway through the European club season, leading to recurring disputes over the release of African players.

Fifa general secretary Mattias Grafstrom was sitting aside Motsepe when the plan was announced, and critics highlighted that the scheduling change favoured football's world governing body more than the African game.

"I think the general sentiment around the continent has been that the two-year cycle has served the continent very well," Football Association of Zambia (Faz) official Sydney Mungala told the BBC.

"The idea of pushing it to a four-year cycle was a bit of a surprise, maybe a concern, to the bulk of the African federations."

Afcon to return to two-year cycle after Caf U-turn

Afcon to be held every four years from 2028

Afcon has developed into Caf's biggest revenue generator, with a profit of $114m (£85m) forecast for Afcon 2025, up from $75m (£56m) for the previous finals in Ivory Coast.

In its stead, an annual Africa Nations League involving all 54 countries on the continent was proposed. Motsepe described the ambition as creating a "world-class competition every year".

The idea was to move beyond Caf's heavy reliance on Afcon and develop a more sustainable commercial model which could support football development.

Yet the last time an ambitious alternative competition took place in Africa, it failed to deliver on its financial promise and was quickly ditched.

The Africa Super League, announced by Caf in 2022 to revolutionise continental club competition, and with projected annual revenues of $200m (£149m), was discontinued after just one edition.

Motsepe later acknowledged that commercial deals fell short of expectations.

"We didn't proceed as quickly because the partners that were giving us money were not giving us the deals we thought we would be happy with," he said.

The decision to move to a four-year cycle was taken at a meeting of Caf's executive committee last December - without being tabled at a general assembly where all member nations are represented.

"These kinds of decisions should be put to the general assembly, they should be debated and discussed for months at a time," Algerian journalist Maher Mezahi told the BBC.

"Afcon is the locomotive by which Caf funds all of its other competitions."

Caf subsequently asked its 54 associations to express a preference between proceeding with the four-year format or retaining the original schedule, and the executive committee eventually voted to restore the status quo.

Motsepe said the decision was in the "best interest of African football" and would contribute to the development and growth of the sport.

He also admitted misgivings about the new Nations League, with concerns it would require "several years" before it could make "the substantial financial and football development contributions" to help the continental game be "self-supporting".

In July Caf president Patrice Motsepe (right) said that Fifa counterpart Gianni Infantino had been "loyal to Africa"

Fifa president Gianni Infantino first publicly proposed holding Afcon every four years in February 2020, an idea Motsepe rejected after he was elected as Caf president 13 months later.

That has not stopped the South African cultivating a close relationship with his counterpart and Infantino's drive to expand the Fifa World Cup to 48 teams - and in the process increase African representation at the tournament - has won him backing across the continent.

Yet the Swiss' position has been under threat since his plan to sell stakes in Fifa's competitions was leaked in July.

Since then Infantino has been busy shoring up his power base ahead of his re-election bid, including at Caf's strategy meeting this month.

"He came to Cape Verde to generate support and, by and large, Africa gave him that support," Mezahi said.

"But I think they did that in a quid pro quo - they gave him the support in return for some concessions.

"And I think the main concession was the return of the Africa Cup of Nations [to a two-year cycle].

"It shows that Africa is willing to assert its influence and look after its interests, even in the face of the global game's interest."

Infantino says he is backed by 'vast majority'

Does Africa still back Infantino as Fifa president?

The 2019 Afcon, won by Algeria, was hosted at the end of the European club season in June and July, but weather conditions saw the 2021 and 2023 editions hosted in a January-February slot while the 2025 Fifa Club Word Cup meant the 2025 finals were pushed back to start in December

Afcon is Caf's financial lifeline, accounting for a substantial share of the governing body's income.

Morocco 2025 was projected to generate $192m (£143m), representing 66% of Caf's total revenue from competitions across men's, women's and age-group football.

For many FAs, Afcon's importance extends far beyond the tournament because they cannot always rely on consistent government or corporate investment.

"We have 11 [Zambian] national teams and only two are partly sponsored by government," Faz official Mungala said.

"The rest have to be supported from the FA's coffers. We actually fund some of these programmes from the support that we get from Caf and Fifa."

Kenya's new 60,000-seater Talanta Stadium, which will host matches at Afcon 2027, is set to be inaugurated with a friendly between European giants Ajax and Bayern Munich in January

The 2027 Afcon is scheduled to be held in Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda from 19 June to 17 July next year.

Yet, on a visit to East Africa in September, Motsepe called for a "heightened sense of urgency" in order to make sure stadiums and supporting infrastructure are ready on time.

The following Afcon will be held just one year later in 2028 - a decision Caf made when planning for the switch to a four-year cycle and which it has stuck with.

An announcement on where and exactly when the finals will be held is yet to be made.

Subsequent tournaments will be held in 2031 and 2033 to avoid clashes with the World Cup.

The proposed kick-off date for the Africa Nations League, meanwhile, is September 2029.

Motsepe's latest statement suggests the new competition will also be held every two years - rather than annually as he initially announced last December – but that begs the question of how space will be found for the fixtures to be played in an Afcon year from 2031 onwards.

While debate continues around the game's congested calendar, Caf's U-turn on scheduling has at least protected the tradition of Africa's biggest sporting showcase.

It also exposes, however, the challenge of finding a workable financial model which benefits African football as well as the demands of the global game.

MN202610_136g7nc9446.t:
Yiech Pur Biel (left) is leading the first ever refugee team at the Youth Olympics

When he started running, Yiech Pur Biel had to compete barefoot. Far from home in a new country, it was the first step towards rebuilding his life as a refugee.

"That's when I decided now it is time to depend on myself and also to start a new life with determination," he tells BBC Newsbeat.

In 2016, Biel made history competing in the 800m event as part of the first Olympic refugee team at the Rio summer Olympics in Brazil.

Ten years on, he's making history again leading the first refugee team for the Youth Olympics as their Chef de Mission.

Joining almost 3,000 athletes, the small team of six will be wanting to make sure their debut counts - but Biel says they're also hoping to send a message that "refugees still need our help".

Hosted in Senegal, Saturday's opening ceremony will launch the first ever Olympic sporting event on African soil.

Africa is home to nearly 45 million displaced people, out of almost 120 million globally, representing the world's biggest displacement crisis.

Biel says for the refugee team, the Youth Olympics is "a chance for them to tell the world and also to represent the population, especially the refugee population, in Africa".

"It's about representing the hope of young people who are living in a refugee camp, who have lost their motivation or their talent."

Biel competed in the first ever refugee team in Rio 2016 and says his new role is an honour

Biel was a child when he was forced to flee his home in South Sudan after his village was attacked.

He ended up in Kenya, telling BBC Newsbeat: "It traumatised me, starting a new life, being alone in Kakuma," referring to the major refugee settlement close to the border between Kenya and South Sudan.

"But I started a new life, I believe that school helped me a lot. It helped me to interact with young people who faced the same challenges."

The rest of his childhood was spent on the refugee camp where he took an interest in football.

After realising it wasn't the sport for him, he gave running a go during trials set up by the International Olympic Committee - where he raced without shoes.

It made him "believe that if I can work harder by myself, I can achieve", he says.

Arno Yafunga Botay is one of six athletes competing for the Refugee Olympic Team at the Dakar 2026 Youth Games

One of the athletes on the refugee team, Arno Yafunga Botay, also lived at Kakuma after fleeing his home in the Democratic Republic of Congo in 2017, when he was six.

Now 15, he will be competing in judo and told BBC Sport Africa he's promised to bring back a gold medal which he'd like to take to the refugee camp.

"I think if I achieve [a] gold medal, I can go there and teach them the value of judo," he said.

As for Biel, he says it's an honour to be chosen as the team's Chef de Mission.

"This is so important for them, to learn from my experience as an athlete and also as a refugee who is coming from a refugee camp," he says.

"So this role means a lot to me and also means a lot to those young athletes who are going to compete."

Competition at Dakar 2026 begins later, with the opening ceremony on Saturday.

MN202610_xri4oua23g.t:
Senegal were initial winners of Afcon 2025 before the result was overturned in favour of Morocco

The Africa Cup of Nations (Afcon) will return to its traditional two-year cycle after a U-turn from the Confederation of African Football (Caf).

In December, Caf announced that the tournament would be held every four years instead, but that decision has been reversed after a review.

Under the new plans, the governing body was planning an African Nations League to replace Afcon as its biennial tournament, but acknowledged that it would take several years to generate the revenue required to become self-sufficient.

"The decision by the Executive Committee to reinstate the organisation of the Afcon every two years aims to advance, protect and promote the interests of African football and the 54 Caf Member Associations, as well as those of African players playing for clubs outside the continent," Caf president Patrice Motsepe said in a statement.

The biennial hosting of Afcon has long caused issues with the football calendar, with the vast majority of recent tournaments held midway through the European club season.

Fifa's expanded 32-team Club World Cup was held in June and July last year, which also forced Caf to opt for mid-season dates.

The next Afcon will take place in 2027, with Kenya, Tanzania and Uganda jointly hosting the tournament, followed by editions in 2028, 2031 and 2033. There will be no tournament in 2030 because of the World Cup.

The dramatic 2025 Afcon final saw Senegal crowned champions before they were stripped of their title three months later in favour of Morocco.

World Service , · 30 Oct 2026 , · 26 mins

Rosemary Nyirumbe became a nun when she was just in her mid-teens – and she felt her true vocation lay in rehabilitating children who had been through some of the worst trauma imaginable. So that’s what she did. In this episode Mike Wooldridge hears Sr Rosemary’s astonishing story. The feared rebel group, the Lord’s Resistance Army, started to terrorise the north of Uganda in the 1980s. Many children, girls as well as boys, were abducted and forced to become child soldiers. In many cases, the LRA forced them to commit atrocities, leaving them deeply traumatised. Many of the girls also bore the children of rebel leaders. As they started to return home, these children were often rejected by their families and communities, says Sr Rosemary. So she set about giving them a future and a hope: through enabling them to acquire skills like sewing, and by helping them see that God had not rejected them for the atrocities they had been forced to commit. More than once, Sr Rosemary put herself in enormous danger in order to fulfil her mission. But, she says, she also learnt that small acts of kindness can touch the hearts of even battle-hardened rebels.
